canonical_title: Fermion sign problem: existence of a polynomial-cost Monte Carlo method for quantum-degenerate fermions
canonical_statement: Can fermionic path integral Monte Carlo, or any related equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo method, compute thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermionic systems with computing cost that does not grow exponentially with particle number N and inverse temperature beta, given that the fermion sign problem causes an exponential increase of computing time and is NP-hard in the general case?
definitions: Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods evaluate finite-temperature properties of interacting quantum many-body systems by sampling configurations of a path-integral or series representation of the partition function. For bosons and many spin systems the configuration weights are non-negative and the sampling is efficient. For fermions, antisymmetrization of the density matrix forces some configuration weights to be negative (or complex), so the weights cannot be used directly as a probability distribution. This is the fermion sign problem.

The standard workaround reweights with respect to the bosonic (absolute-value) reference ensemble, at the price that statistical errors are amplified by the inverse average sign. For quantum-degenerate fermions the average sign behaves as $S = \exp(-\beta N \Delta f)$, where $\Delta f$ is a free-energy-density difference between the fermionic and reference ensembles, $N$ is the particle number, and $\beta$ is the inverse temperature. Because Monte Carlo error bars shrink only as $1/\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{MC}}}$ in the number of samples, the compute time needed to hold accuracy fixed grows exponentially in $N$ and $\beta$, producing the exponential wall documented in detail for path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) of degenerate electrons.

Troyer and Wiese (Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 170201 (2005)) showed that the sign problem in general is NP-hard: they exhibited a class of quantum systems (a spin-glass-like model) for which removing the sign problem with polynomial overhead would allow all problems in the complexity class NP to be solved in polynomial time. Hence a generic polynomial-cost solution of the sign problem would imply P = NP, which is widely believed false but unproven. This bounds what a 'generic solution' would mean, but it does not by itself settle the existence question for the full equilibrium Monte Carlo setting, nor does it preclude either a stronger hardness theorem covering that setting directly or a construction that somehow circumvents the reduction's assumptions.

Later literature has produced substantial partial progress without closing the question: sign-problem-free subclasses identified through symmetry and sign-structure analysis (e.g. Majorana representations, antiunitary-symmetry-protected models), complex-path and Lefschetz-thimble methods, contour-deformation and machine-learned manifolds, sign-mitigation schemes (sign blocking, Bogoliubov-inequality bounds, permutation-blocking), and the recent discovery of models with only algebraic rather than exponential decay of the average sign. Review-level treatments through 2024 (Alexandru et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 94, 015006 (2022); Pan and Meng, Encyclopedia of Condensed Matter Physics, 2nd ed. (2024)) continue to present the sign problem as an unsolved fundamental barrier. An unrefereed preprint claim of a complete generic solution (Wang and Sun, arXiv:2203.04070) has not been accepted by the community and is inconsistent with the known basis-dependence analyses.

The unresolved target, faithful to the source formulation, is therefore: does there exist an equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo method (PIMC or related) that computes thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermionic systems in full generality — no restriction to a particular model, ensemble, or temperature window — with computing cost that does not grow exponentially with particle number $N$ and inverse temperature $\beta$? A positive answer requires a constructed method with demonstrated sub-exponential cost scaling in the general fermionic setting; a negative answer requires a rigorous impossibility or conditional-hardness result extending beyond the known special-case NP-hardness.
scope: Equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo methods (PIMC and related approaches) applied to quantum-degenerate fermionic systems in full generality — no restriction to a particular model, ensemble, or temperature window; the question is whether the exponential scaling of cost with particle number and inverse temperature can be circumvented, given that a generic solution is known to be NP-hard.
aliases: Negative sign problem in quantum Monte Carlo
Polynomial-time solution of the sign problem

authoritative_formulation.citation: M. Troyer and U.-J. Wiese, Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations, Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 170201 (2005), arXiv:cond-mat/0408370
authoritative_formulation.exact_excerpt: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations, while being efficient for bosons, suffer from the "negative sign problem'' when applied to fermions - causing an exponential increase of the computing time with the number of particles. A polynomial time solution to the sign problem is highly desired since it would provide an unbiased and numerically exact method to simulate correlated quantum systems. Here we show, that such a solution is almost certainly unattainable by proving that the sign problem is NP-hard, implying that a generic solution of the sign problem would also solve all problems in the complexity class NP (nondeterministic polynomial) in polynomial time.

formulation_change.rationale: No major later progress narrows or reframes the source question. Review-level literature through 2024 (Alexandru et al. RMP 2022; Pan and Meng 2024) confirms the Troyer-Wiese NP-hardness as the standing rigorous result and treats generic polynomial-cost fermionic Monte Carlo as unsolved; partial progress (sign-free subclasses, thimbles, sign mitigation, algebraic-sign models) targets special cases or eases the exponent without touching the general existence question. The one claimed generic solution (Wang and Sun, arXiv:2203.04070) is an unaccepted preprint and does not constitute community-recognized closure. Canonical title, statement, scope, and answer types are therefore frozen.

literature_treatment: Later literature uniformly treats the fermion sign problem as a fundamental, unsolved barrier. The Reviews of Modern Physics review by Alexandru, Basar, Bedaque, and Warrington (2022) frames complex-path/thimble methods as partial attacks on a problem that blocks Monte Carlo for dense matter, the doped repulsive Hubbard model, and real-time observables — i.e., the problem is presented as open. The Pan and Meng encyclopedia chapter (2024) reviews cures, easements, and exploitations of the sign problem, including basis optimization, symmetry-protected sign-free classes, and algebraic-sign regimes, while making clear these are model-specific and do not amount to a generic polynomial solution. Troyer-Wiese NP-hardness remains the canonical rigorous statement and is cited in current work (2025-2026 arXiv literature) as the reason a generic solution is not expected. A 2022 preprint by Wang and Sun claims a complete generic solution, but it remains unrefereed, has not been adopted or validated in the subsequent review literature, and postdates reviews that continue to state the problem as unsolved; it cannot be counted as closure.
status_rationale: A systematic same-core search (reviews, forward-citation context of Troyer-Wiese in 2025-2026 literature, claimed-solution check) finds no credible closure of the general question and no narrowing that applies to the source's full generality. All rigorous progress is either the original NP-hardness (which bounds but does not settle the equilibrium Monte Carlo existence question) or special-case sign-free constructions that the source explicitly does not accept as the general answer. The surviving core is therefore the original question unchanged. Confidence is medium rather than high because the LKM route was unavailable in this environment (gaia CLI not installed), so coverage rests on web retrieval; and because 'still open' here is inferred from how review-level literature treats the core rather than from an exhaustive forward-citation chain, though the items inspected are authoritative and recent.
surviving_open_core: Whether any equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo method (fermionic PIMC or a related approach) can compute thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermionic systems in full generality — no model, ensemble, or temperature restriction — with computing cost that does not grow exponentially with particle number N and inverse temperature beta. The known special-case NP-hardness (Troyer-Wiese) makes a generic polynomial solution imply P = NP, but neither a generic construction nor a hardness theorem covering the full equilibrium Monte Carlo setting exists in the audited literature.
importance_motivation: The candidate is the famous fermion sign problem at full source generality, and later-literature audit confirms it remains the central unsolved barrier of computational many-body physics: current reviews (RMP 2022; Encyclopedia of Condensed Matter Physics 2024) still organize method development around circumventing it, and the exponential wall S = exp(-beta N Delta f) continues to block ab initio simulation of warm dense matter, quantum chemistry, and correlated electron systems. Resolution in either direction — a construction or a general hardness theorem — would materially change the capability frontier or convert a near-universally believed practical barrier into a settled fundamental limit.
scientific_significance_rationale: A positive resolution would deliver an unbiased, numerically exact polynomial-cost method for thermal properties of correlated fermions, directly changing the capability frontier for warm dense matter, quantum chemistry, and correlated electron systems that are currently blocked by the exponential wall S = exp(-beta N Delta f). A negative resolution extending the known general-case NP-hardness to the stated equilibrium Monte Carlo setting would convert a widely believed practical barrier into a settled fundamental limit, redirecting the field's method-development decisions toward controlled approximations. Held back from 10 only because the most probable outcome is a hardness confirmation of a limit the community already treats as near-certain; even that outcome is a decisive bound, and a construction would be field-transforming.
consequences_of_progress: A constructed sub-exponential method would immediately unlock numerically exact equilibrium simulation of warm dense matter (relevant to inertial confinement fusion and planetary interiors), doped Hubbard-type correlated electron models, and finite-temperature quantum chemistry at system sizes currently infeasible by many orders of magnitude. A general impossibility or conditional-hardness theorem would settle methodology debates, justifying permanent investment in controlled approximations (restricted PIMC, density matrix embedding, tensor networks, quantum computing) rather than continued search for a generic classical Monte Carlo cure.
current_best_result: The strongest rigorous result remains Troyer and Wiese (PRL 94, 170201 (2005)): the sign problem is NP-hard in general (via a spin-glass reduction), so a generic polynomial-cost solution would imply P = NP. The strongest constructive results are all special-case: symmetry- and sign-structure-based sign-free fermionic QMC classes (Majorana and antiunitary-symmetry constructions), model-specific algebraic-sign regimes reported by Pan, Meng and collaborators, and mitigation methods (Lefschetz thimbles and contour deformations, sign blocking, permutation blocking, Bogoliubov-inequality path-integral MD) that reduce but do not remove the exponential cost in the general degenerate-fermion setting. No audited work achieves sub-exponential cost for general quantum-degenerate fermions, and no audited work extends the hardness result to cover the full equilibrium Monte Carlo setting as stated.
expected_result: A final submission resolves the source question in one of two committed forms. Either (a) a rigorous impossibility or conditional-hardness theorem establishing that no equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo method can compute thermal properties of general quantum-degenerate fermionic systems with cost sub-exponential in particle number N and inverse temperature beta, stating its assumptions and complexity-theoretic hypotheses explicitly; or (b) a fully specified method accompanied by a correctness argument and a demonstrated, independently checkable sub-exponential cost scaling in N and beta on quantum-degenerate fermionic systems in the general setting, with error bars and systematics documented so the scaling claim, not merely accuracy at one size, is the submitted claim. A method valid only on sign-problem-free subclasses does not constitute the expected result, since the source question commits to the general fermionic setting.
verification_standard: The submission is checked against the original source-faithful question: does an equilibrium Monte Carlo method exist that computes thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermionic systems at cost not growing exponentially in N and beta? Branch (a): a hardness or impossibility proof passes if its stated assumptions are explicit, its reduction or argument is valid under independent derivation review, and its conclusion covers the general fermionic equilibrium setting rather than an isolated model class already known to Troyer-Wiese. Branch (b): a constructed method passes if (i) its correctness argument for fermionic thermal expectation values is sound, and (ii) its cost model or measured cost, checked by independent replay of the pinned protocol with documented error bars and systematics across increasing N and beta, exhibits sub-exponential scaling on quantum-degenerate fermionic systems not restricted to a sign-problem-free special case. A submission passes exactly when one branch withstands this scrutiny; presenting a special-case construction as the general answer fails.
verification_difficulty_rationale: This result genuinely answers the source question because both acceptance branches settle the existence question the sources pose; the residual limit is that a hardness branch may be conditional on standard complexity hypotheses, which the contract requires to be stated, not discharged. Taking the cheapest sound branch of the either-or contract does not help much: neither branch yields a finite witness. A construction's scaling claim is asymptotic in N and beta, so no finite simulation suite certifies it — replay validates consistency, but the load-bearing claim is the correctness-and-scaling argument itself, a connected derivation the Reviewer must reconstruct, including that the cost model honestly counts all sampling effort (the 1/sqrt(N_MC) compensation noted in the source) and that no exponential factor hides in preprocessing, basis choice, or ensemble choice. A hardness proof is likewise a novel, connected derivation whose reduction must be checked step by step, with nontrivial specification-fidelity work to confirm the formalized computational task faithfully encodes equilibrium fermionic Monte Carlo rather than the spin-glass special case of Troyer-Wiese. The load-bearing items a Reviewer must inspect are: the correctness reduction or error analysis, the explicit cost accounting in N and beta, the generality of the fermionic setting relative to the Troyer-Wiese special cases, and any complexity hypotheses. This is a long, novel chain with substantial specification reconstruction: score 8.
solution_review_checklist: Identify which acceptance branch is claimed (hardness/impossibility vs. construction) and confirm the submission explicitly targets the general quantum-degenerate fermionic equilibrium setting, not a sign-problem-free subclass.

For a hardness submission: verify every complexity-theoretic hypothesis is stated explicitly; check the reduction step by step; confirm the formalized computational task faithfully encodes equilibrium fermionic Monte Carlo sampling and is not merely a restatement of the Troyer-Wiese spin-glass case.

For a construction submission: verify the correctness argument for fermionic thermal expectation values (including antisymmetrization handling) and confirm the cost model counts all sampling effort, preprocessing, basis-optimization overhead, and the 1/sqrt(N_MC) statistical compensation.

Check that the claimed sub-exponential scaling is in N and beta jointly for quantum-degenerate systems, with error bars and systematics documented across increasing system sizes — accuracy at a single size is not sufficient.
Independently replay any pinned numerical protocol to confirm reported costs and signs are reproducible, while recognizing replay supports but cannot by itself certify the asymptotic scaling claim.
Confirm no exponential factor is hidden in ensemble choice, reference-system construction, or problem-instance selection.
estimated_solution_review_time: Four to eight weeks of expert review for either branch; a novel hardness reduction or a full correctness-plus-scaling argument for a new method each require reconstruction of a long, nonstandard derivation plus independent replay of the pinned numerical protocol.
acceptance_boundary: Accept exactly when one branch withstands independent scrutiny at full source generality: (a) a valid, explicit-hypothesis hardness or impossibility argument covering the general equilibrium fermionic Monte Carlo setting, or (b) a constructed method with a sound correctness argument and independently replayed sub-exponential cost scaling in N and beta on quantum-degenerate fermions. Reject special-case sign-free constructions presented as the general answer, reformulations that hide the exponential cost in an uncounted step, scaling claims supported only at fixed size, and hardness arguments that merely restate the known Troyer-Wiese special cases.
ci_pseudocode: Placeholder: no automated checker exists for either acceptance branch. A hardness/impossibility proof is a novel mathematical argument requiring human derivation review; a construction's asymptotic sub-exponential scaling claim cannot be certified by any terminating finite procedure. If a construction is submitted, a partial checker could replay the submitter's pinned simulation protocol (fixed code, seeds, and N/beta grid) to recompute costs, average signs, and error bars and compare them against the reported scaling data — this validates consistency of the reported numbers but not the asymptotic claim itself.
ci_estimated_runtime: not applicable — no implemented CI; hypothetical protocol replay would scale with the submitter's largest reported system size

compute.expected_scale: not applicable for the hardness branch; for a construction branch, verification replay scales with the largest demonstrated fermionic system sizes (moderate to large HPC depending on the submitted protocol)
compute.cpu: Review itself needs no compute; optional replay of a submitted construction protocol could require the same CPU resources the submission reports (potentially thousands of core-hours for large N and low temperature)
compute.gpu: none required for verification; a submission may use GPUs in its protocol, in which case replay would need comparable access
compute.notes: Compute is contingent on a construction-type submission and is pinned by its own protocol; there is no standing CI workload. Verification burden is dominated by derivation review, not computation.

evidence.title: Complex paths around the sign problem (Rev. Mod. Phys. 94, 015006)
evidence.supports: Direct: abstract of the authoritative 2022 Reviews of Modern Physics review inspected. It presents the sign problem as the standing obstacle that makes dense matter, the doped repulsive Hubbard model, and real-time observables inaccessible to Monte Carlo 'as it currently stands', and reviews thimble/complex-path methods as partial attacks with successes limited to specific examples — i.e., the general problem is treated as open, not solved.

evidence.title: Sign Problem in Quantum Monte Carlo Simulation (Encyclopedia of Condensed Matter Physics, 2nd ed., 2024)
evidence.supports: Direct: abstract of the 2024 encyclopedia chapter by Pan and Meng inspected. It surveys efforts to 'cure, ease and even make use of' the sign problem — symmetry analysis, basis optimization, algebraic-sign regimes — all explicitly model- or basis-dependent, confirming that no generic polynomial-cost solution exists and that progress consists of special-case circumventions rather than a general answer.

evidence.title: Computational Complexity and Fundamental Limitations to Fermionic Quantum Monte Carlo Simulations (Phys. Rev. Lett. 94, 170201)
evidence.supports: Direct: abstract of Troyer and Wiese inspected; it is the authoritative formulation of the named problem and supplies the standing rigorous result — the sign problem is NP-hard in general, so a generic polynomial solution would imply P = NP. This remains the best result on the question and bounds rather than settles the equilibrium Monte Carlo existence question.

evidence.title: A Generic Solution of Fermion Sign Problem
evidence.supports: Contested claim: preprint by Wang and Sun claims the sign problem is 'completely solved' via positive-weight path replacement, applied to the 2D Hubbard model. It remains unrefereed (v6, May 2022), is not cited as a resolution in the subsequent review literature (including the 2024 Pan-Meng chapter, which continues to treat the problem as unsolved), and resembles basis-reformulation approaches known not to yield generic polynomial cost. Recorded so the claim is visible; it cannot be counted as closure.

evidence.title: Quantum critical points and the sign problem (Science 375, 418)
evidence.supports: Supplementary: Mondaini, Tarat, and Scalettar connect the sign problem to quantum critical phenomena, treating it as a fundamental physical property of the model rather than a removable artifact; cited in 2025-2026 literature alongside Troyer-Wiese. Metadata level only — included as context that current research continues to investigate, not resolve, the sign problem.
